statement: A net of six squares folds into a cube. One square is shaded. Which square ends up opposite the shaded one?

figure.alt: A net of six squares in a cross shape: a vertical column of four squares labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 from the top, with square 5 attached to the left of square 2 and square 6 attached to the right of square 2. Square 1 is shaded.

choices.misconception: I picked the square directly next to the shaded one in the net, but neighbours in the net share an edge on the cube.
I counted to the far end of the column, assuming the square furthest away in the net is the one opposite.
I picked one of the side flaps because it is not touching the shaded square in the drawing.
I picked the other side flap for the same reason, without tracking what happens as the net folds.

hints: In a strip, opposite faces are two apart.
Fold the four-square column into a ring around the cube. In a ring of four faces, each face is opposite the one two steps along, not the one next to it and not the one at the end.

Squares 1, 2, 3, 4 form a ring around the cube. Going round the ring, 1 is opposite 3 and 2 is opposite 4. Squares 5 and 6 become the remaining pair, top and bottom. So the shaded square 1 is opposite square 3.

solutions.reliable: The column of four squares wraps into a ring around the cube. Walk around that ring: 1, 2, 3, 4, then back to 1. Two faces are opposite when they are two steps apart in the ring, so 1 faces 3 and 2 faces 4. The two flaps, 5 and 6, take the last pair of opposite faces. The shaded square 1 is therefore opposite square 3. The transferable idea: find the ring of four first, then read opposites two apart.
solutions.elegant: In any cube net, two squares two apart in a straight strip always land opposite each other, so you can read the answer without folding anything.

whyOnTest: Nets separate students who track one face through the fold from students who judge by how far apart the squares look on the page.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
